The figure summarizes a network of microbial processes that drive nitrogen, carbon, and sulfur cycling, apparently in low-oxygen marine conditions. It highlights how different groups of microbes are linked by exchanged compounds such as ammonia, nitrite, nitrate, methane, sulfide, oxygen, and dinitrogen.

Across the top, denitrification converts organic matter plus nitrate into nitrogen gases, while anammox combines ammonium and nitrite to form N2. A separate pathway shows heterotrophic nitrogen fixation, where organic carbon and oxygen or nitrate support conversion of N2 into ammonia.

The middle portion emphasizes small amounts of oxygen, shown as “trace O2,” produced by photosynthesis and supplied by advection. That oxygen seems to enable nitrification, with Thaumarchaeota oxidizing ammonia to nitrite and Nitrospina/Nitrococcus oxidizing nitrite to nitrate. Trace oxygen also supports methane oxidation by Methylococcales, while NC10 bacteria are shown coupling methane oxidation to nitrite reduction, producing N2 and oxygen internally.

The bottom portion depicts sulfur cycling. Sulfate reducers generate sulfide from organic carbon and sulfate, and sulfur-oxidizing microbes use sulfide with nitrate or nitrous oxide, producing oxidized sulfur, N2, and sometimes N2O. Overall, the diagram shows tightly interconnected redox metabolisms sustained by scarce oxygen and recycling between elemental pools.
